item.title: The Booster Catch SpaceX Called Off: How Starship's Own Launch Blinded Its Tower
item.description: On Flight 6 a Super Heavy booster was minutes from the second tower catch ever when the launch itself damaged the tower. Why SpaceX sent the booster into the sea instead, and how that caution paid off.

item.title: How SpaceX Catches Both Halves of Starship: Why the Ship Takes 22 Hours and the Booster 7 Minutes
item.description: On Flight 15 SpaceX plans to catch the Super Heavy booster after about 6.5 minutes and the ship about 22.5 hours later, at the same tower. Here is why the ship has to wait almost a whole day.

item.title: Musk Once Mocked Flying Cars. How Tesla's Roadster Took Nine Years to Fly Anyway
item.description: In 2017 Elon Musk called flying cars noisy and dangerous; that same year he unveiled a Roadster that would end up flipping in midair. The story of the thruster tweet, nine years of slipped dates and the flight.

item.title: How Does Tesla's 'Flying' Roadster Actually Fly? Fans, Nitrogen Thrusters and the Math
item.description: The new Tesla Roadster drove upside down and flipped over a Semi. Here is how its suction fans and SpaceX-style nitrogen thrusters do it, and why it can only stay up for seconds.

item.title: From six free solar stations to 85,000 plugs: how Tesla's Superchargers outlived the team that built them
item.description: In 2012 Tesla opened six solar-powered chargers and promised Model S owners free charging forever. Here is how that network crossed a continent, opened to rivals, survived the firing of almost its entire team, and became the hardest part of Tesla to copy.

item.title: Why Does a Tesla Battery Have Thousands of Small Cells? From Laptop Cells to the 4680
item.description: The first Tesla ran on 6,831 laptop cells; a Cybertruck stores twice the energy in 1,344. Why Tesla builds packs from small cylinders, what makes the 4680 different, and whether it matters when you buy.

item.title: Four minutes and a crater: how Starship's disastrous first flight taught SpaceX to catch rockets
item.description: In April 2023 Starship's first flight lasted four minutes, wrecked its own launch pad and had to be blown up. This is how that failure set up the attempt to catch both halves of the rocket.

item.title: How Does a Tesla Robotaxi Keep Its Cameras Clean? Washers, Wipers and Lasers Explained
item.description: A Robotaxi has no driver to wipe a dirty lens. Here is how Tesla keeps its cameras clean today, what its 'eyelid' and laser patents describe, and what it means for owners.

item.title: Catching $6 million falling from space: how SpaceX's net boat Mr. Steven chased rocket nose cones, and why it quit
item.description: For almost three years SpaceX tried to catch falling Falcon 9 nose cones in a giant net on a boat. It finally worked in 2019, then the company gave it up. The story explains why, and what it means for catching Starship.

item.title: Why Does Starship Have 33 Engines Instead of One Giant One?
item.description: The Soviet N1 failed with 30 engines and Apollo's giant F-1 took years to tame. Here is why SpaceX's Super Heavy uses 33 Raptors, and why it works where the N1 did not.

item.title: Two Crashes, One Explosion, Then It Landed: How SpaceX Brought Back Its First Orbital Rocket in 2015
item.description: In 2015 SpaceX crashed two boosters on its landing ship and lost a whole rocket before a Falcon 9 first stage finally flew back and landed upright in Florida. The story of that first landing, and why it still matters for Starship.

item.title: How Much Does It Cost to Send 1 kg Into Space? From the Space Shuttle to Starship
item.description: The fuel for a Starship flight works out to about 9 dollars a kilo, yet the Space Shuttle cost about 54,500. Here is why, how Falcon 9 cut the price, and what Starship needs to get under 100 dollars a kilo.

item.title: Tesla Semi Interior Explained: Why the Driver Sits in the Middle, and What a Day in the Cab Looks Like
item.description: Inside the Tesla Semi: the center seat, the two 16-inch screens, the jump seat and the missing bed, and how charging fits a driver's legal breaks in the US and Europe.

item.title: What Happens to Your Tesla When Tesla Stops Making It? Cybertruck, Model S and X Explained
item.description: Tesla is ending the Cybertruck after the Model S and X. What that means for warranty, parts, service, software updates and resale value, with lessons from the original Roadster.

item.title: The Truck That Broke Its Own Window: Why the Cybertruck Looks Like That, and How Tesla's Steel Bet Played Out
item.description: From a cracked window on stage in 2019 to the end of production at Giga Texas: the story of the stainless steel bet behind the Cybertruck, what it cost Tesla and what it leaves behind.

item.title: Why Does Starship Fire Its Engines at Its Own Booster? Hot Staging Explained
item.description: Starship lights its six engines while it is still attached to the Super Heavy booster. Here is how hot staging works, why it adds payload, who did it first and what it means for catching both stages.

item.title: 5,000 Model 3s in a Week: The Tent That Saved Tesla From Production Hell
item.description: In June 2018, close to running out of money, Tesla built a whole Model 3 assembly line in a tent on its parking lot. How it happened, whether it worked, and why it still shapes how Tesla builds cars.

item.title: Can the Tesla Cybercab Drive in Europe? Why a Car With No Steering Wheel Needs New Rules
item.description: Tesla's Cybercab is touring Europe, but nobody can ride it. How European type approval works, why driverless cars are capped at 1,500 a year, and what has to change first.

item.title: Dealt like a deck of cards: how SpaceX launched its first 60 Starlink satellites without a single spring
item.description: In 2019 SpaceX stacked 60 flat satellites in one rocket and simply let them drift apart. The story of the rushed bet that became the blueprint for every Starlink launch, and why it matters to Tesla.

item.title: How SpaceX catches Starship: why the ship has no wings, no legs and no parachutes
item.description: SpaceX wants to catch both Starship stages with its launch tower. How a ship without wings falls belly first, flips upright and lands in the tower's arms, why that is harder than catching the booster, and how it lands on the Moon instead.

item.title: Why the Tesla Semi took nine years: from a 2017 stage promise to its own factory and Europe's roads
item.description: Promised for 2019 with 500 miles of range and sports-car acceleration, the Tesla Semi was delayed by battery shortages, proved its range in a 1,076-mile day and now heads for Europe. The story of the truck, and the one promise still open.

item.title: Is There a Tesla Phone? The Model Pi Rumor vs What Musk and Starlink Are Really Building
item.description: Viral videos promise a solar-charged Tesla Model Pi with Starlink built in. Here is what Tesla and Musk have actually said, how Starlink is coming to ordinary phones instead, and how to spot a fake.

item.title: How SpaceX caught a 232-foot rocket with 'chopsticks': the story of the first Super Heavy catch
item.description: Super Heavy was built without landing legs, betting everything on a tower that could catch it in midair. How the idea was born, how the first catch in October 2024 worked, and why it matters for every Starship flight since.

item.title: Grok does the mapping, you do the napping?
item.description: Grok can plan your route and Tesla FSD can drive it, but you may not sleep at the wheel. What each system does, why napping is not allowed yet, and when it could be.

item.title: The Lotus that became the first Tesla: how the original Roadster nearly broke the company
item.description: Tesla's first car was meant to be a quick electric conversion of a Lotus Elise. In the end only about 7% of the Lotus survived, the costs exploded, and the Roadster still started everything Tesla is today.

item.title: Tesla's Emergency Drive Away gets its first real use, and an accidental tap reportedly brings a $539 service bill
item.description: A month after launch, a Model Y driver in Austin drove off a Supercharger with the cable attached, and an owner who never moved the car was reportedly told it costs $539 to clear the alert.

item.title: What is Tesla FSD (Supervised)? What it does, what it costs and where you can use it
item.description: Tesla's Full Self-Driving (Supervised) explained: what the system really does, why you must keep watching, the monthly price in the US, UK, Europe and Australia, and the countries where it is allowed as of October 2026.

item.title: Tesla halves its China down payment to 39,900 yuan on zero-interest Model 3 and Model Y loans
item.description: Until November 30, Chinese buyers can finance a Model 3, Model Y or Model Y L over five years at 0% with half the usual down payment, as Tesla's sales in China keep falling.

item.title: Italy backs EU-wide approval of Tesla FSD after Salvini's call with Musk, putting the 65% vote bar within reach
item.description: Italy's transport minister says Rome supports a swift EU approval of Tesla Assisted Driving. With Germany already on board, Tesla now has a path past the EU's population rule, but only just.

item.title: Tesla Robotaxi now runs until 2 a.m., adding trip sharing, Calm Mode, a live rear camera and Grok in Model Y
item.description: Tesla's driverless ride service now operates from 6 a.m. to 2 a.m., 20 hours a day. The update also adds features aimed at night riders, but Tesla has not said which cities get the new hours.
